subject: English
title: A Letter to the Brave
hook: Through heartfelt letters, ordinary citizens—children, grandmothers, and farmers—express gratitude to soldiers serving far from home.

slides.title: A Letter to the Brave
slides.storyContext: A school campaign encourages students to write letters to soldiers posted in remote areas. Through their words, a bridge of gratitude and humanity forms between civilians and those who serve.

image.alt: A Letter to the Brave — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: The Letter Campaign
slides.storyContext: Priya's teacher announces a project: write a letter to an unknown soldier serving in Ladakh, Siachen, or the northeast. Priya decides to write about her ordinary day—school, cricket, family dinner—so the soldier knows what he's protecting.
slides.inSimpleWords: Priya realizes soldiers are human; they miss home just like anyone would.

image.alt: The Letter Campaign — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: Why Words Matter

points.text: A soldier in a freezing Siachen glacier can receive a letter and feel warmth from a stranger's gratitude.
Words remind soldiers of home, of the normal lives they left behind, of the reason they serve.
A simple 'Thank you' can lift a soldier's spirits on the hardest days.

example.problem: Priya doesn't know Captain Rajesh. What should she write to a complete stranger?
example.solution: She writes: 'Dear Captain, I'm a 7th grader in Delhi. Today I had samosa with chai, played cricket, and laughed with friends. I know you're on a glacier protecting our border so I can live safely. Thank you for being brave so I can be free.'

slides.inSimpleWords: Soldiers are humans who feel loneliness, homesickness, and need encouragement.

image.alt: Why Words Matter — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: The Reality of Military Life

points.text: Soldiers are posted in harsh conditions: Siachen at -60°C, the Kargil mountains, dense forests.
They live far from families for years, eating bland rations, sleeping in tents.
They face danger, loneliness, and the constant weight of responsibility.

slides.inSimpleWords: Soldiers give up comfort and safety to guard ours.

image.alt: The Reality of Military Life — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: Different Letters, Same Heart

points.text: Grandma Savitri writes: 'My son served 40 years ago. Receiving one letter kept him alive through a difficult winter.' She encourages Priya to write more.
A farmer writes: 'Captain, my fields are safe because of your courage. My gratitude is endless.'
Each letter, from child or elder, from farmer or shopkeeper, carries the voice of the nation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every person's gratitude matters—children, parents, grandparents, all of India speaks.

image.alt: Different Letters, Same Heart — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: Humanity in Service

points.text: A soldier is not just a uniform—he or she is a person with dreams, fears, and a family.
Captain Rajesh reads Priya's letter during a difficult night watch and remembers he has purpose.
He writes back: 'Dear Priya, your letter reminded me why I serve. Tell me more about your life. Let me feel connected to home.'

slides.inSimpleWords: Behind the uniform is a human heart that needs to know they are valued.

image.alt: Humanity in Service — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: Building Understanding

points.text: Through letters, civilians learn that soldiers are not just warriors—they are protectors, often young, often frightened.
Through letters, soldiers learn that their sacrifice is seen and appreciated.
Letters break down the distance between the battlefield and home.

slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding brings compassion; letters create that bridge.

image.alt: Building Understanding — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: The Power of One Letter
slides.storyContext: Captain Rajesh received Priya's letter during the coldest month in Ladakh. He was struggling with frostbite and thinking of quitting. Her words—'You are my hero because you stand guard while I sleep'—reminded him of his purpose. He returned home safely and visited Priya's school to thank her personally.
slides.inSimpleWords: One letter from one girl changed one soldier's entire perspective.

image.alt: The Power of One Letter — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: Write Your Own Letter
slides.storyContext: Write a letter to a soldier—real or imagined. Tell them about your day, your dreams, your gratitude. Describe something that makes you laugh or something you enjoy. Help them feel connected to the life they protect.

example.problem: What would you say to a soldier you've never met?
example.solution: You might write: 'Dear Jawan, I'm a 7th grader who wants to be a doctor. I read your life is hard. But your sacrifice makes my dreams possible. The least I can do is become excellent at something. Thank you for believing in my future when I do.'

slides.inSimpleWords: Your words have power. A soldier reading them will know they matter.

image.alt: Write Your Own Letter — My Dear Soldiers

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Soldiers are humans—they miss home, feel fear, and need encouragement.
A simple letter can lift a soldier's spirit on the hardest days.
Every person's gratitude—from children to elders—strengthens the nation.
Understanding soldiers as human beings builds respect and compassion.
Words create bridges across the distance between home and the battlefield.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your words can reach a soldier's heart and remind them why they serve.

image.alt: What We Learned — My Dear Soldiers

subject: English
title: A Queen's Defiance
hook: In 16th-century India, a woman warrior-queen resists colonial conquest with courage and strategic brilliance, becoming a legend of resistance.

slides.title: A Queen's Defiance
slides.storyContext: In 16th-century South India, Rani Abbakka Devi ruled Vitality. When Portuguese colonizers arrived with cannons and greed, she did what few dared: she said no and fought back with intelligence, courage, and unyielding determination.

image.alt: A Queen's Defiance — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: The Rise of Abbakka
slides.storyContext: Abbakka was born into a merchant family in coastal Karnataka in the 1520s. When her husband died, she became regent for her young son. But when Portuguese colonizers demanded tribute and threatened to impose their rule, Abbakka made a revolutionary decision: she would resist, even if it meant war.
slides.inSimpleWords: Abbakka refused to surrender her kingdom to foreign conquerors.

image.alt: The Rise of Abbakka — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: Understanding Colonization

points.text: In the 16th century, European powers (Portuguese, Dutch, British) came to India seeking trade and territory.
They didn't ask for permission—they took by force, claiming 'civilization' and 'progress' as justification.
Most Indian rulers either welcomed them for trade advantages or surrendered without fight.

example.problem: The Portuguese commander demands: 'Pay us tribute and we'll allow you to trade.' Abbakka refuses. Why?
example.solution: She says: 'I am Rani, not a servant. My kingdom is mine. I will trade as equals, not as a subject to a master. If you want my land, you must earn it through honorable means, not extortion.'

slides.inSimpleWords: Abbakka valued freedom over safety; dignity over compromise.

image.alt: Understanding Colonization — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: A Woman's Authority

points.text: In the 1500s, women rarely held power. Men assumed they were too weak for leadership or war.
Abbakka broke this stereotype. She trained as a warrior, studied strategy, and commanded armies.
She proved that courage and intelligence know no gender.

slides.inSimpleWords: Abbakka showed that a woman's mind and courage are as powerful as any man's.

image.alt: A Woman's Authority — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: The Battle Strategy

points.text: The Portuguese had cannons and ships. Abbakka had fewer soldiers but knew the coastline.
She built fortifications using the terrain, trained soldiers in guerrilla tactics, and cut supply lines.
In 1555, she defeated a Portuguese invasion. In 1557, she did it again. And again in 1569.

example.problem: The Portuguese have superior weapons. How can Abbakka defeat them?
example.solution: She learns their patterns, ambushes their supply convoys, fortifies mountain passes, and uses the sea against them. She turns their advantage into a weakness by fighting on terrain she controls.

slides.inSimpleWords: Intelligence and knowledge of the land matter more than powerful weapons.

image.alt: The Battle Strategy — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: Personal Cost of Resistance

points.text: Abbakka's defiance came at a price. Her kingdom faced constant attacks and economic hardship.
She watched young soldiers die defending her border. She slept little, ate little, worried constantly.
But she never wavered. She believed freedom was worth the price.

slides.inSimpleWords: True resistance requires sacrifice. Abbakka paid it without complaint.

image.alt: Personal Cost of Resistance — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: Legacy of Defiance

points.text: Abbakka ruled for 40 years, never letting the Portuguese conquer her kingdom.
She died in 1574, but her resistance inspired generations of Indians to fight colonization.
Centuries later, Indians would remember: if one woman can resist empires, so can we.

slides.inSimpleWords: Abbakka showed that resistance is possible even against overwhelming odds.

image.alt: Legacy of Defiance — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: A Queen's Letter
slides.storyContext: Abbakka once wrote to the Portuguese commander: 'You come to my land with arrogance, believing might makes right. But my ancestors ruled here for generations. My people have tilled this soil, fished these waters, and built these forts. This is our home. You are the invader, and invaders do not stay.' She signed it with her seal and sent it with a warrior. The Portuguese never forgot her defiance.
slides.inSimpleWords: Abbakka's words were as powerful as her sword.

image.alt: A Queen's Letter — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: Standing Firm for What You Believe
slides.storyContext: Abbakka faced an empire but refused to bend. In your own life, you may face smaller battles—peer pressure, unjust rules, or situations where doing the right thing is hard. What would Abbakka do? How can you apply her courage to your challenges?

example.problem: Your friends want you to cheat on a test. Everyone's doing it, but you know it's wrong. What would Abbakka do?
example.solution: Like Abbakka facing the Portuguese alone, you stand firm. You say no, even if you're alone. You believe in your values. In the end, integrity—like Abbakka's kingdom—remains standing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Courage means standing alone for what's right.

image.alt: Standing Firm for What You Believe — Rani Abbakka

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Rani Abbakka was one of the first to resist European colonization in India.
She proved that women can be brilliant strategists, fearless warriors, and visionary leaders.
Resistance requires intelligence, courage, sacrifice, and unwavering belief in your cause.
One person's defiance can inspire generations and change history.
Abbakka's legacy reminds us that standing up for freedom is always worth the cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Abbakka was a queen who refused to bow. History remembers her with honor.

image.alt: What We Learned — Rani Abbakka

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank
title: Priya's Growing Piggy Bank
hook: A young girl learns why banks pay her for keeping money safe.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A curious Class 7 student who opens her first bank account

characters.name: Mr. Sharma
characters.role: The friendly bank manager at Local Bank

characters.name: Avi
characters.role: Priya's older brother, who explains pocket-money savings

image.alt: Priya's Growing Piggy Bank — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: The Mystery of Extra Money
slides.storyContext: Priya has saved ₹1,000 from her birthday and Diwali money. Avi says, 'Put it in a bank account, it will grow!' Priya wonders, 'How can money grow? It's not a plant!' She visits Local Bank to find out.

image.alt: The Mystery of Extra Money — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: What Is Interest?
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma explains: 'When you give us your money, we lend it to farmers, shopkeepers, and families who need it. They pay us back extra money for using it. We share that extra money with YOU. That extra is called interest.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Interest is the money a bank GIVES you for keeping your money safe with them.

points.label: Why?
points.text: The bank uses your money to help others (loans) and keeps a part of the profit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Banks say: 'Thank you for trusting us with your money. Here's a gift (interest) for being smart.'

image.alt: What Is Interest? — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: Principal — Your Starting Money
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma points to Priya's account: 'This ₹1,000 you put in is the PRINCIPAL. The bank will add interest to it every year. But the principal amount stays YOUR money to take out anytime.'

points.label: Principal (P)
points.text: The original money you deposit in the bank.

points.label: Example
points.text: Priya puts ₹1,000 → Principal = ₹1,000

slides.inSimpleWords: Principal is the money YOU put in. The bank doesn't take it; it just borrows it and pays you interest.

image.alt: Principal — Your Starting Money — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: Rate of Interest — The Percentage
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma shows a chart on the wall: 'Different accounts earn different interest. Savings Account = 4% per year. Fixed Deposit = 6% per year. The percentage is the RATE.'

points.label: Rate of Interest (R)
points.text: The percentage of principal the bank gives you as interest each year.

points.label: Common rates
points.text: Savings Account: 3-5%. Fixed Deposit: 5-7%. These change with market.

slides.inSimpleWords: The rate is 'how generous the bank is.' Higher rate = more interest earned.

image.alt: Rate of Interest — The Percentage — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: Time — How Long You Keep Money
slides.storyContext: Avi asks Mr. Sharma, 'If Priya keeps ₹1,000 for 1 year vs. 2 years, does she earn more interest?' Mr. Sharma nods: 'Yes! The longer you save, the more interest grows.'

points.label: Time (T)
points.text: How long you keep the principal in the bank (usually in years).

points.label: Logic
points.text: More time = more interest earned (the bank has more time to use your money).

slides.inSimpleWords: Time is your patience. The longer you wait, the richer you get!

image.alt: Time — How Long You Keep Money — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: Simple Interest Formula
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma writes on a whiteboard: 'I'll show you the magic formula. Simple Interest = (P × R × T) ÷ 100. That's it! With this, you can calculate exactly how much interest you earn.'

points.label: Where
points.text: P = Principal (₹), R = Rate (%), T = Time (years), SI = Simple Interest (₹)

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply principal, rate, and time, then divide by 100. That's your interest!

image.alt: Simple Interest Formula — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: Priya's Interest — A Worked Example
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma pulls out a calculator: 'Let's find out how much interest Priya earns. She deposits ₹1,000 in a Savings Account at 4% interest for 1 year.'

example.problem: Priya puts ₹1,000 in a bank account. The bank offers 4% simple interest per year. How much interest does she earn in 1 year? What will be her total amount after 1 year?
example.solution:
Given: P = ₹1,000, R = 4%, T = 1 year.
Step 1: SI = (P × R × T) ÷ 100
Step 2: SI = (1,000 × 4 × 1) ÷ 100
Step 3: SI = 4,000 ÷ 100 = ₹40
Step 4: Total Amount = Principal + Interest = ₹1,000 + ₹40 = ₹1,040
Answer: Priya earns ₹40 as interest. Her total after 1 year is ₹1,040.

image.alt: Priya's Interest — A Worked Example — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: Your Turn — Avi's Challenge
slides.storyContext: Avi says to Priya: 'I have ₹2,500 in a Fixed Deposit at 5% interest for 2 years. Can you calculate my interest?' Priya takes out her notebook and tries to solve it.

example.problem: Avi deposits ₹2,500 in a Fixed Deposit at 5% simple interest per year. How much interest will he earn in 2 years?
example.solution:
Given: P = ₹2,500, R = 5%, T = 2 years.
SI = (P × R × T) ÷ 100
SI = (2,500 × 5 × 2) ÷ 100
SI = 25,000 ÷ 100 = ₹250
Answer: Avi earns ₹250 as interest in 2 years. Total amount = ₹2,750.

image.alt: Your Turn — Avi's Challenge — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

slides.title: Smart Saving Tips from Mr. Sharma
slides.storyContext: Before leaving, Mr. Sharma shares wisdom: 'Interest is like a magic word—the sooner you start saving, the more magic happens. Time is your best friend.'

points.label: Start early
points.text: Even ₹500 today grows faster than ₹5,000 later (because of time).

points.label: Higher rate, better growth
points.text: Compare accounts: Fixed Deposits earn more than Savings Accounts.

points.label: Keep it longer
points.text: Don't withdraw early; let interest add up.

slides.inSimpleWords: The three secrets: Start now, pick a good rate, and wait patiently.

image.alt: Smart Saving Tips from Mr. Sharma — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank

points.text: Interest is money the bank gives you for keeping your money safe.
Principal (P) = the money you deposit.
Rate (R) = percentage interest per year.
Time (T) = how many years you save.
Simple Interest (SI) = (P × R × T) ÷ 100.
More principal, higher rate, and longer time = more interest.

image.alt: What Priya Learned — Interest — How Money Grows in a Bank
